entries.e518408e70d461c012acc82d88118845103507e5: <div sID="gen2677" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="27" osisID="Lev.27" sID="Lev.27"/> <div eID="gen2677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2678" type="x-p"/> The <reference osisRef="Lev.26.46">last verse of the foregoing chapter</reference> seemed to close up the statute-book; yet this chapter is added as an appendix. Having given laws concerning instituted services, here he directs concerning vows and voluntary services, the free-will offerings of their mouth. Perhaps some devout serious people among them might be so affected with what Moses had delivered to them in the foregoing chapter as in a pang of zeal to consecrate themselves, or their children, or estates to him: this, because honestly meant, God would accept; but, because men are apt to repent of such vows, he leaves room for the redemption of what had been so consecrated, at a certain rate. Here is, I. The law concerning what was sanctified to God, persons (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.2-Lev.27.8">ver. 2-8</reference>), cattle, clean or unclean (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.9-Lev.27.13">ver. 9-13</reference>), houses and lands (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.15-Lev.27.25">ver. 15-25</reference>), with an exception of firstlings, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.26-Lev.27.27">ver. 26, 27</reference>. II. Concerning what was devoted, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.28-Lev.27.29">ver. 28, 29</reference>. III. Concerning tithes, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.30-Lev.27.34">ver. 30</reference>, &c.
entries.d0044dc6fabca80eb85ee7431782cbc12211decf: <div eID="gen2678" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Law Concerning Vows. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2679" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When a man shall make a singular vow, the persons <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> by thy estimation. <hi type="super">3</hi> And thy estimation shall be of the male from twenty years old even unto sixty years old, even thy estimation shall be fifty shekels of silver, after the shekel of the sanctuary. <hi type="super">4</hi> And if it <hi type="italic">be</hi> a female, then thy estimation shall be thirty shekels. 5 And if <hi type="italic">it be</hi> from five years old even unto twenty years old, then thy estimation shall be of the male twenty shekels, and for the female ten shekels. <hi type="super">6</hi> And if <hi type="italic">it be</hi> from a month old even unto five years old, then thy estimation shall be of the male five shekels of silver, and for the female thy estimation <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> three shekels of silver. <hi type="super">7</hi> And if <hi type="italic">it be</hi> from sixty years old and above; if <hi type="italic">it be</hi> a male, then thy estimation shall be fifteen shekels, and for the female ten shekels. <hi type="super">8</hi> But if he be poorer than thy estimation, then he shall present himself before the priest, and the priest shall value him; according to his ability that vowed shall the priest value him. <hi type="super">9</hi> And if <hi type="italic">it be</hi> a beast, whereof men bring an offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , all that <hi type="italic">any man</hi> giveth of such unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall be holy. <hi type="super">10</hi> He shall not alter it, nor change it, a good for a bad, or a bad for a good: and if he shall at all change beast for beast, then it and the exchange thereof shall be holy. <hi type="super">11</hi> And if <hi type="italic">it be</hi> any unclean beast, of which they do not offer a sacrifice unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , then he shall present the beast before the priest: <hi type="super">12</hi> And the priest shall value it, whether it be good or bad: as thou valuest it, <hi type="italic">who art</hi> the priest, so shall it be. <hi type="super">13</hi> But if he will at all redeem it, then he shall add a fifth <hi type="italic">part</hi> thereof unto thy estimation. <div eID="gen2679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2680" type="x-p"/> This is part of the law concerning singular vows, extraordinary ones, which though God did not expressly insist on, yet, if they were consistent with and conformable to the general precepts, he would be well pleased with. Note, We should not only ask, What must we do, but, What may we do, for the glory and honour of God? As the <hi type="italic">liberal devises liberal things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.8">Isa. xxxii. 8</reference>), so the pious devises pious things, and the enlarged heart would willingly do something extraordinary in the service of so good a Master as God is. When we receive or expect some singular mercy it is good to honour God with some singular vow. <div eID="gen2680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2681" type="x-p"/> I. The case is here put of persons vowed to God by a singular vow, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.2">v. 2</reference>. If a man consecrated himself, or a child, to the service of the tabernacle, to be employed there in some inferior office, as sweeping the floor, carrying out ashes, running of errands, or the like, <hi type="italic">the person</hi> so consecrated <hi type="italic">shall be for the Lord,</hi> that is, "God will graciously accept the good-will." <hi type="italic">Thou didst well that it was in thy heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.8">2 Chron. vi. 8</reference>. But forasmuch as he had no occasion to use their service about the tabernacle, a whole tribe being appropriated to the use of it, those that were thus vowed were to be redeemed, and the money paid for their redemption was employed for the repair of the sanctuary, or other uses of it, as appears by <reference osisRef="2Kgs.12.14">2 Kings xii. 14</reference>, where it is called, in the margin, the <hi type="italic">money of the souls of his estimation.</hi> A book of rates is accordingly provided, by which the priests were to go in their estimation. Here is, 1. The rate of the middle-aged, between twenty and threescore, these were valued highest, because most serviceable; a male fifty shekels, and a female thirty, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.3-Lev.27.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. The females were then less esteemed, but not so in Christ; for in <hi type="italic">Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.28">Gal. iii. 28</reference>. Note, Those that are in the prime of their time must look upon themselves as obliged to do more in the service of God and their generation than can be expected either from minors, that have not yet arrived to their usefulness, or from the aged, that have survived it. 2. The rate of the youth between five years old and twenty was less, because they were then less capable of doing service, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.5">v. 5</reference>. 3. Infants under five years old were capable of being vowed to God by their parents, even before they were born, as Samuel was, but not to be presented and redeemed till a month old, that, as one sabbath passed over them before they were circumcised, so one new moon might pass over them before they were estimated; and their valuation was but small, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.6">v. 6</reference>. Samuel, who was thus vowed to God, was not redeemed, because he was a Levite, and a particular favourite, and therefore was employed in his childhood in the service of the tabernacle. 4. The aged are valued less than youth, but more than children, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.7">v. 7</reference>. And the Hebrews observe that the rate of an aged woman is two parts of three to that of an aged man, so that in that age the female came nearest to the value of the male, which occasioned (as bishop Patrick quotes it here) this saying among them, <hi type="italic">That an old woman in a house is a treasure in a house.</hi> Paul sets a great value upon the aged women, when he makes them <hi type="italic">teachers of good things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.2.3">Tit. ii. 3</reference>. 5. The poor shall be valued according to their ability, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.8">v. 8</reference>. Something they must pay, that they might learn not to be rash in vowing to God, for <hi type="italic">he hath no pleasure in fools,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.4">Eccl. v. 4</reference>. Yet not more than their ability, but <hi type="italic">secundum tenementum—according to their possessions,</hi> that they might not ruin themselves and their families by their zeal. Note, God expects and requires from men according to what they have, and not according to what they have not, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.4">Luke xxi. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen2681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2682" type="x-p"/> II. The case is put of beasts vowed to God, 1. If it was a clean beast, such as was offered in sacrifice, it must not be redeemed, nor any equivalent given for it: <hi type="italic">It shall be holy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.27.9-Lev.27.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. After it was vowed, it was not to be put to any common use, nor changed upon second thoughts; but it must be either offered upon the altar, or, if through any blemish it was not meet to be offered, he that vowed it should not take advantage of that, but the priests should have it for their own use (for they were God's receivers), or it should be sold for the service of the sanctuary. This teaches caution in making vows and constancy in keeping them when they are made; for <hi type="italic">it is a snare to a man to devour that which is holy, and after vows to make enquiry,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.25">Prov. xx. 25</reference>. And to this that rule of charity seems to allude (<reference osisRef="2Cor.9.7">2 Cor. ix. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Every man, according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give.</hi> 2. If it was an unclean beast, it should go to the use of the priest at such a value; but he that vowed it, upon paying that value in money, and adding a fifth part more to it, might redeem it if he pleased, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.11-Lev.27.13">v. 11-13</reference>. It was fit that men should smart for their inconstancy. God has let us know his mind concerning his service, and he is not pleased if we do not know our own. God expects that those that deal with him should be at a point, and way what they will stand to.
entries.e52765b9e963ce824c6cbf3277d546a6fb136749: <div eID="gen2682" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Concerning Things Sanctified. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2683" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> And when a man shall sanctify his house <hi type="italic">to be</hi> holy unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , then the priest shall estimate it, whether it be good or bad: as the priest shall estimate it, so shall it stand. <hi type="super">15</hi> And if he that sanctified it will redeem his house, then he shall add the fifth <hi type="italic">part</hi> of the money of thy estimation unto it, and it shall be his. <hi type="super">16</hi> And if a man shall sanctify unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">some part</hi> of a field of his possession, then thy estimation shall be according to the seed thereof: an homer of barley seed <hi type="italic">shall be valued</hi> at fifty shekels of silver. <hi type="super">17</hi> If he sanctify his field from the year of jubilee, according to thy estimation it shall stand. <hi type="super">18</hi> But if he sanctify his field after the jubilee, then the priest shall reckon unto him the money according to the years that remain, even unto the year of the jubilee, and it shall be abated from thy estimation. <hi type="super">19</hi> And if he that sanctified the field will in any wise redeem it, then he shall add the fifth <hi type="italic">part</hi> of the money of thy estimation unto it, and it shall be assured to him. 20 And if he will not redeem the field, or if he have sold the field to another man, it shall not be redeemed any more. <hi type="super">21</hi> But the field, when it goeth out in the jubilee, shall be holy unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , as a field devoted; the possession thereof shall be the priest's. <hi type="super">22</hi> And if <hi type="italic">a man</hi> sanctify unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> a field which he hath bought, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> not of the fields of his possession; <hi type="super">23</hi> Then the priest shall reckon unto him the worth of thy estimation, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto the year of the jubilee: and he shall give thine estimation in that day, <hi type="italic">as</hi> a holy thing unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">24</hi> In the year of the jubilee the field shall return unto him of whom it was bought, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to him to whom the possession of the land <hi type="italic">did belong.</hi> <hi type="super">25</hi> And all thy estimations shall be according to the shekel of the sanctuary: twenty gerahs shall be the shekel. <div eID="gen2683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2684" type="x-p"/> Here is the law concerning real estates dedicated to the service of God by a singular vow. <div eID="gen2684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2685" type="x-p"/> I. Suppose a man, in his zeal for the honour of God, should <hi type="italic">sanctify his house to God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.14">v. 14</reference>), the house must be valued by the priest, and the money got by the sale of it was to be converted to the use of the sanctuary, which by degrees came to be greatly enriched with <hi type="italic">dedicated things,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.15">1 Kings xv. 15</reference>. But, if the owner be inclined to redeem it himself, he must not have it so cheap as another, but must add a fifth part to the price, for he should have considered before he had vowed it, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.15">v. 15</reference>. To him that was necessitous God would abate the estimation (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.8">v. 8</reference>); but to him that was fickle and humoursome, and whose second thoughts inclined more to the world and his secular interest than his first, God would rise in the price. Blessed be God, there is a way of sanctifying our houses to be holy unto the Lord, without either selling them or buying them. If we and our houses serve the Lord, if religion rule in them, and we put away iniquity far from them, and have a church in our house, holiness to the Lord is written upon it, it is his, and he will dwell with us in it. <div eID="gen2685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2686" type="x-p"/> II. Suppose a man should sanctify some part of his land to the Lord, giving it to pious uses, then a difference must be made between land that came to the donor by descent and that which came by purchase, and accordingly the case altered. <div eID="gen2686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2687" type="x-p"/> 1. If it was the inheritance of his fathers, here called the <hi type="italic">field of his possession,</hi> which pertained to his family from the first division of Canaan, he might not give it all, no, not to the sanctuary; God would not admit such a degree of zeal as ruined a man's family. But he might sanctify or dedicate only some part of it, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.16">v. 16</reference>. And in that case, (1.) The land was to be valued (as our countrymen commonly compute land) by so many measures' sowing of barley. So much land as would take a <hi type="italic">homer,</hi> or <hi type="italic">chomer,</hi> of barley, which contained ten ephahs, <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.11">Ezek. xlv. 11</reference> (not, as some have here mistaken it, an <hi type="italic">omer,</hi> which was but a tenth part of an ephah, <reference osisRef="Exod.16.36">Exod. xvi. 36</reference>), was valued at fifty shekels, a moderate price (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.16">v. 16</reference>), and that if it were sanctified immediately from the year of jubilee, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.17">v. 17</reference>. But, if some years after, there was to be a discount accordingly, even of that price, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.18">v. 18</reference>. And, (2.) When the value was fixed, the donor might, if he pleased, redeem it for sixty shekels the homer's sowing, which was with the addition of a fifth part: the money then went to the sanctuary, and the land reverted to him that had sanctified it, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.19">v. 19</reference>. But if he would not redeem it, and the priest sold it to another, then at the year of jubilee, beyond which the sale could not go, the land came to the priests, and was theirs for ever, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.20-Lev.27.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. Note, What is given to the Lord ought not to be given with a power of revocation; what is devoted to the Lord must be his for ever, by a perpetual covenant. <div eID="gen2687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2688" type="x-p"/> 2. If the land was his own purchase, and came not to him from his ancestors, then not the land itself, but the value of it was to be given to the priests for pious uses, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.22">v. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.24">24</reference>. It was supposed that those who, by the blessing of God, had grown so rich as to become purchasers would think themselves obliged in gratitude to sanctify some part of their purchase, at least (and here they are not limited, but they might, if they pleased, sanctify the whole), to the service of God. For we ought to give <hi type="italic">as God prospers us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.2">1 Cor. xvi. 2</reference>. Purchasers are in a special manner bound to be charitable. Now, forasmuch as purchased lands were by a former law to return at the year of jubilee to the family from which they were purchased, God would not have that law and the intentions of it defeated by making the lands <hi type="italic">corban, a gift,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.11">Mark vii. 11</reference>. But it was to be computed how much the land was worth for so many years as were from the vow to the jubilee; for only so long it was his own, and God <hi type="italic">hates robbery for burnt-offerings.</hi> We can never acceptably serve God with that of which we have wronged our neighbour. And so much money he was to give for the present, and keep the land in his own hands till the year of jubilee, when it was to return free of all encumbrances, even that of its being dedicated to him of whom it was bought. The value of the shekel by which all these estimations were to be made is here ascertained (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.25">v. 25</reference>); it shall be twenty gerahs, and every gerah was sixteen barley-corns. This was fixed before (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.13">Exod. xxx. 13</reference>); and, whereas there had been some alterations, it is again fixed in the laws of Ezekiel's visionary temple (<reference osisRef="Ezek.45.12">Ezek. xlv. 12</reference>), to denote that the gospel should reduce things to their ancient standard.
entries.b28c3b94f4e0c7ba10db2a05db216cec42f210f8: <div eID="gen2688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2689" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> Only the firstling of the beasts, which should be the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's firstling, no man shall sanctify it; whether <hi type="italic">it be</hi> ox, or sheep: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's. <hi type="super">27</hi> And if <hi type="italic">it be</hi> of an unclean beast, then he shall redeem <hi type="italic">it</hi> according to thine estimation, and shall add a fifth <hi type="italic">part</hi> of it thereto: or if it be not redeemed, then it shall be sold according to thy estimation. <hi type="super">28</hi> Notwithstanding no devoted thing, that a man shall devote unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of all that he hath, <hi type="italic">both</hi> of man and beast, and of the field of his possession, shall be sold or redeemed: every devoted thing <hi type="italic">is</hi> most holy unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">29</hi> None devoted, which shall be devoted of men, shall be redeemed; <hi type="italic">but</hi> shall surely be put to death. <hi type="super">30</hi> And all the tithe of the land, <hi type="italic">whether</hi> of the seed of the land, <hi type="italic">or</hi> of the fruit of the tree, <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's: <hi type="italic">it is</hi> holy unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . 31 And if a man will at all redeem <hi type="italic">ought</hi> of his tithes, he shall add thereto the fifth <hi type="italic">part</hi> thereof. <hi type="super">32</hi> And concerning the tithe of the herd, or of the flock, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of whatsoever passeth under the rod, the tenth shall be holy unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">33</hi> He shall not search whether it be good or bad, neither shall he change it: and if he change it at all, then both it and the change thereof shall be holy; it shall not be redeemed. <hi type="super">34</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the commandments, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses for the children of Israel in Mount Sinai. <div eID="gen2689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2690" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A caution given that no man should make such a jest of sanctifying things to the Lord as to sanctify any firstling to him, for that was his already by the law, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.26">v. 26</reference>. Though the matter of a general vow be that which we were before obliged to, as of our sacramental covenant, yet a singular vow should be of that which we were not, in such circumstances and proportions, antecedently bound to. The law concerning the firstlings of unclean beasts (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.27">v. 27</reference>) is the same with that before, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.11-Lev.27.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. <div eID="gen2690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2691" type="x-p"/> II. Things or persons devoted are here distinguished from things or persons that were only sanctified. 1. Devoted things were most holy to the Lord, and could neither revert nor be alienated, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.28">v. 28</reference>. They were of the same nature with those sacrifices which were called most holy, which none might touch but only the priests themselves. The difference between these and other sanctified things arose from the different expression of the vow. If a man dedicated any thing to God, binding himself with a solemn curse never to alienate it to any other purpose, then it was a thing devoted. 2. Devoted persons were to be put to death, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.29">v. 29</reference>. Not that it was in the power of any parent or master thus to devote a child or a servant to death; but it must be meant of the public enemies of Israel, who, either by the appointment of God or by the sentence of the congregation, were devoted, as the seven nations with which they must make no league. The city of Jericho in particular was thus devoted, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.17">Josh. vi. 17</reference>. The inhabitants of Jabesh-Gilead were put to death for violating the curse pronounced upon those who came not up to Mizpeh, <reference osisRef="Judg.21.9-Judg.21.10">Judg. xxi. 9, 10</reference>. Some think it was for want of being rightly informed of the true intent and meaning of this law that Jephtha sacrificed his daughter as one devoted, who might not be redeemed. <div eID="gen2691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2692" type="x-p"/> III. A law concerning tithes, which were paid for the service of God before the law, as appears by Abraham's payment of them, (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.20">Gen. xiv. 20</reference>), and Jacob's promise of them, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.22">Gen. xxviii. 22</reference>. It is here appointed, 1. That they should pay tithe of all their increase, their corn, trees, and cattle, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.30">v. 30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.32">32</reference>. Whatsoever productions they had the benefit of God must be honoured with the tithe of, if it were titheable. Thus they acknowledged God to be the owner of their land, the giver of its fruits, and themselves to be his tenants, and dependents upon him. Thus they gave him thanks for the plenty they enjoyed, and supplicated his favour in the continuance of it. And we are taught in general to <hi type="italic">honour the Lord with our substance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.9">Prov. iii. 9</reference>), and in particular to support and maintain his ministers, and to be <hi type="italic">ready to communicate</hi> to them, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.6">Gal. vi. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.11">1 Cor. ix. 11</reference>. And how this may be done in a fitter and more equal proportion than that of the tenth, which God himself appointed of old, I cannot see. 2. That which was once marked for tithe should not be altered, no, not for a better (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.33">v. 33</reference>), for Providence directed the rod that marked it. God would accept it though it were not the best, and they must not grudge it though it were, for it was what passed under the rod. 3. That it should not be redeemed, unless the owner would give a fifth part more for its ransom, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.31">v. 31</reference>. If men had the curiosity to prefer what was marked for tithe before any other part of their increase, it was fit that they should pay for their curiosity. <div eID="gen2692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2693" type="x-p"/> IV. The <reference osisRef="Lev.27.34">last verse</reference> seems to have reference to this whole book of which it is the conclusion: <hi type="italic">These are the commandments which the Lord commanded Moses, for the children of Israel.</hi> Many of these commandments are moral, and of perpetual obligation; others of them, which were ceremonial and peculiar to the Jewish economy, have notwithstanding a spiritual significancy, and are instructive to us who are furnished with a key to let us into the mysteries contained in them; for <hi type="italic">unto us,</hi> by those institutions, <hi type="italic">is the gospel preached as well as unto them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.4.2">Heb. iv. 2</reference>. Upon the whole matter, we may see cause to bless God that <hi type="italic">we have not come to Mount Sinai,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.18">Heb. xii. 18</reference>. 1. That we are not under the <hi type="italic">dark shadows</hi> of the law, but enjoy the clear light of the gospel, which shows us <hi type="italic">Christ the end of the law for righteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.10.4">Rom. x. 4</reference>. The doctrine of our reconciliation to God by a Mediator is not clouded with the smoke of burning sacrifices, but cleared by the knowledge of <hi type="italic">Christ and him crucified.</hi> 2. That we are not under the <hi type="italic">heavy yoke</hi> of the law, and the carnal ordinances of it (as the apostle calls them, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.10">Heb. ix. 10</reference>), imposed till the time of reformation, a yoke which <hi type="italic">neither they nor their fathers were able to bear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.10">Acts xv. 10</reference>), but under the sweet and easy institutions of the gospel, which pronounces those the <hi type="italic">true worshippers that worship the Father in spirit and truth,</hi> by Christ only, and in his name, who is our priest, temple, altar, sacrifice, purification, and all. Let us not therefore think that because we are not tied to the ceremonial cleansings, feasts, and oblations, a little care, time, and expense, will serve to honour God with. No, but rather have our hearts more enlarge with free-will offerings to his praise, more inflamed with holy love and joy, and more engaged in seriousness of thought and sincerity of intention. <hi type="italic">Having boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, let us draw near with a true heart, and full assurance of faith,</hi> worshipping God with so much the more cheerfulness and humble confidence, still saying, <hi type="italic">Blessed be God for Jesus Christ!</hi>  <chapter eID="Lev.27"/> <div eID="gen2693" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen2233" osisID="Lev" type="book"/>

entries.589a333de91a2cdd76b2950704a7e02815d5e0e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1225"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 27</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.27.1-Lev.27.18">Le 27:1-18</reference>. Concerning Vows.</title> <div sID="gen1669" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1225"/><hi type="bold">2-8. When a man shall make a singular vow, &c.--</hi>Persons have, at all times and in all places, been accustomed to present votive offerings, either from gratitude for benefits received, or in the event of deliverance from apprehended evil. And Moses was empowered, by divine authority, to prescribe the conditions of this voluntary duty.<div eID="gen1669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1670" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the persons shall be for the Lord, &c.--</hi>better rendered thus:--"According to thy estimation, the persons shall be for the Lord." Persons might consecrate themselves or their children to the divine service, in some inferior or servile kind of work about the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="1Sam.3.1">1Sa 3:1</reference>). In the event of any change, the persons so devoted had the privilege in their power of redeeming themselves; and this chapter specifies the amount of the redemption money, which the priest had the discretionary power of reducing, as circumstances might seem to require. Those of mature age, between twenty and sixty, being capable of the greatest service, were rated highest; young people, from five till twenty, less, because not so serviceable; infants, though devotable by their parents before birth (<reference osisRef="1Sam.1.11">1Sa 1:11</reference>), could not be offered nor redeemed till a month after birth; old people were valued below the young, but above children; and the poor--in no case freed from payment, in order to prevent the rash formation of vows--were rated according to their means. <div eID="gen1670" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b753f33ca63dcb21a4b91fd9f904fda44ea8888: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1226"/><div sID="gen1671" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1226"/><hi type="bold">9-13. if it be a beast, whereof men bring an offering unto the Lord--</hi>a clean beast. After it had been vowed, it could neither be employed in common purposes nor exchanged for an equivalent--it must be sacrificed--or if, through some discovered blemish, it was unsuitable for the altar, it might be sold, and the money applied for the sacred service. If an unclean beast--such as an ass or camel, for instance, had been vowed, it was to be appropriated to the use of the priest at the estimated value, or it might be redeemed by the person vowing on payment of that value, and the additional fine of a fifth more. <div eID="gen1671" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6af71b762b6b00b45b306f7ffc486a04708c3e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1227"/><div sID="gen1672" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1227"/><hi type="bold">14-15. when a man shall sanctify his house to be holy unto the Lord, &c.--</hi>In this case, the house having been valued by the priest and sold, the proceeds of the sale were to be dedicated to the sanctuary. But if the owner wished, on second thought, to redeem it, he might have it by adding a fifth part to the price. <div eID="gen1672" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3f1444c7d0ee0a62c7475b332318e9f6b4b160d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1228"/><div sID="gen1673" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1228"/><hi type="bold">16-24. if a man shall sanctify unto the Lord some aprt of a field of his possession, &c.--</hi>In the case of acquired property in land, if not redeemed, it returned to the donor at the Jubilee; whereas the part of a hereditary estate, which had been vowed, did not revert to the owner, but remained attached in perpetuity to the sanctuary. The reason for this remarkable difference was to lay every man under an obligation to redeem the property, or stimulate his nearest kinsman to do it, in order to prevent a patrimonial inheritance going out from any family in Israel. <div eID="gen1673" type="x-p"/>
entries.008fab87ff53e8062515bf8db1c52967e40828ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1229"/><div sID="gen1674" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1229"/><hi type="bold">26-27. Only the firstling of the beasts--</hi>These, in the case of clean beasts, being consecrated to God by a universal and standing law (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.12">Ex 13:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.19">34:19</reference>), could not be devoted; and in that of unclean beasts, were subject to the rule mentioned (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.11">Le 27:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen1674" type="x-p"/>
entries.1cd04948207610c0f389cac8ec2217bf0732a90a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1230"/><div sID="gen1675" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1230"/><hi type="bold">28-29. no devoted thing, that a man shall devote unto the Lord of all that he hath, ... shall be sold or redeemed--</hi>This relates to vows of the most solemn kind--the devotee accompanying his vow with a solemn imprecation on himself not to fail in accomplishing his declared purpose. <div eID="gen1675" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4f6df2a237fbb425180dbdd6a02d9f7a5e496c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1232"/><div sID="gen1677" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1232"/><hi type="bold">30-33. all the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land--</hi>This law gave the sanction of divine authority to an ancient usage (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.20">Ge 14:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.28.22">28:22</reference>). The whole produce of the land was subjected to the tithe tribute--it was a yearly rent which the Israelites, as tenants, paid to God, the owner of the land, and a thank offering they rendered to Him for the bounties of His providence. (See <reference osisRef="Prov.3.9">Pr 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.11">1Co 9:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.6">Ga 6:6</reference>). <div eID="gen1677" type="x-p"/>
entries.b66838af9c47ea82095ac3680e6852aaadab05fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1234"/><div sID="gen1679" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1234"/><hi type="bold">34. These are the commandments, &c.--</hi>The laws contained in this book, for the most part ceremonial, had an important spiritual bearing, the study of which is highly instructive (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.4">Ro 10:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.2">He 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.18">12:18</reference>). They imposed a burdensome yoke (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.10">Ac 15:10</reference>), but yet in the infantine age of the Church formed the necessary discipline of "a schoolmaster to Christ" [Ga 3:24]. <chapter eID="Lev.27"/><div eID="gen1679" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen1354" osisID="Lev" type="book"/>

entries.2d4c38495408b9648ee1021dc142e437659dc63b: <div eID="gen5074" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen5075" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5076" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5076" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5075" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5077" type="x-p"/> Laws concerning vows, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.1">Lev 27:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.2">Lev 27:2</reference>. Of males and females from twenty to sixty years of age, and their valuation, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.3">Lev 27:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.4">Lev 27:4</reference>. Of the same from five to twenty years, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.5">Lev 27:5</reference>. Of the same from a month to five years of age, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.6">Lev 27:6</reference>. Of males and females from sixty years old and upwards, and their valuation, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.7">Lev 27:7</reference>. The priest shall value the poor according to his ability, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.8">Lev 27:8</reference>. Concerning beasts that are vowed, and their valuation, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.9-Lev.27.13">Lev 27:9-13</reference>. Concerning the sanctification of a house, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.14">Lev 27:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.15">Lev 27:15</reference>. Concerning the field that is sanctified or consecrated to the Lord, to the year of jubilee, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.16-Lev.27.24">Lev 27:16-24</reference>. Every estimation shall be made in shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.25">Lev 27:25</reference>. The firstlings of clean beasts, being already the Lord's, cannot be vowed, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.26">Lev 27:26</reference>. That of an unclean beast may be redeemed, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.27">Lev 27:27</reference>. Every thing devoted to God shall be unalienable and unredeemable, and continue the Lord's property till death, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.28">Lev 27:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.29">Lev 27:29</reference>. All the tithe of the land is the Lord's, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.30">Lev 27:30</reference>; but it may be redeemed by adding a fifth part, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.31">Lev 27:31</reference>. The tithe of the herd and the flock is also his, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.32">Lev 27:32</reference>. The tenth that passes under the rod shall not be changed, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.33">Lev 27:33</reference>. The conclusion of the book, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.34">Lev 27:34</reference>.
entries.2a057e9107127ba4dc44fd4352dd889382be5134: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen5077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5078" type="x-p"/> When a man shall make a singular vow - The verse is short and obscure, and may be translated thus: A man who shall have separated a vow, according to thy estimation, of souls unto the Lord; which may be paraphrased thus: He who shall have vowed or consecrated a soul, i. e., a living creature, whether man or beast, if he wish to redeem what he has thus vowed or consecrated, he shall ransom or redeem it according to the priest's estimation; for the priest shall judge of the properties, qualifications, and age of the person or beast, and the circumstances of the person who has vowed it, and shall regulate the value accordingly; and the money shall be put into his hands for the service of the sanctuary. A vow (says Mr. Ainsworth) is a religious promise made unto the Lord, and for the most part with prayer, and paid with thanksgiving, <reference osisRef="Num.21.2">Num 21:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.21.3">Num 21:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.66.12">Psa 66:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.66.14">Psa 66:14</reference>. Vows were either of abstinence, such as are spoken of Numbers 30, and the vow of the Nazarite, Numbers 6; or they were to give something to the Lord, as sacrifices, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.16">Lev 7:16</reference>, or the value of persons, beasts, houses, or lands, concerning which the law is here given. A man might vow or devote himself, his children, (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.5">Lev 27:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.6">Lev 27:6</reference>), his domestics, his cattle, his goods, etc. And in this chapter rules are laid down for the redemption of all these things. But if, after consecrating these things, he refused to redeem them, then they became the Lord's property for ever. The persons continued all their lives devoted to the service of the sanctuary; the goods were sold for the profit of the temple or the priests; the animals, if clean, were offered in sacrifice; if not proper for sacrifice, were sold, and the price devoted to sacred uses. This is a general view of the different laws relative to vows, mentioned in this chapter.
entries.1947162f40558ec09f8f2ad1cd2a316b7d9efb03: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen5078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5079" type="x-p"/> From twenty years old even unto sixty-fifty shekels - A man from twenty to sixty years of age, if consecrated to the Lord by a vow, might be redeemed for fifty shekels, which, at 3s. each, amounted to 7. 10s. sterling.
entries.3852ff072362824a530a64d9531964249d56c2cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen5079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5080" type="x-p"/> And if it be a female - The woman, at the same age, vowed unto the Lord, might be redeemed for thirty shekels, 4. 10s. sterling, a little more than one half of the value of the man; for this obvious reason, that a woman, if employed, could not be of so much use in the service of the sanctuary as the man, and was therefore of much less value.
entries.2e52663bf8e3ee9d8ee5b6d3864cbeeee641be43: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen5080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5081" type="x-p"/> From five years old - The boy that was vowed might be redeemed for twenty shekels, 3. sterling; the girl, for ten shekels, just one half, 1. 10s.
entries.dd2ed4eecde5432c3825b8c7acc343d10fd97c6b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen5081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5082" type="x-p"/> A month old - The male child, five shekels, 15s., the female, three shekels, 9s. Being both in comparative infancy, they were nearly of an equal value. None were vowed under a month old: the first-born being always considered as the Lord's property, could not be vowed, see <reference osisRef="Lev.27.26">Lev 27:26</reference>.
entries.5e7490f1d3a16c8b31457e82290bcae439d30727: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen5082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5083" type="x-p"/> Sixty years old - The old man and the old woman, being nearly past labor, were nearly of an equal value; hence the one was estimated at fifteen shekels, 2. 5s., the other at ten shekels, 1. 10s. This was about the same ratio as that of the children, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.5">Lev 27:5</reference>, and for the same reason.
entries.3caa6b30d3e0bca27eb3a22ff62223502c58960e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen5083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5084" type="x-p"/> He shall not alter it, nor change it, a good for a bad, etc. - Whatever was consecrated to God by a vow, or purpose of heart, was considered from that moment as the Lord's property; to change which was impiety; to withhold it, sacrilege. Reader, hast thou ever dedicated thyself, or any part of thy property, to the service of thy Maker? If so, hast thou paid thy vows? Or hast thou altered thy purpose, or changed thy offering? Has he received from thy hands a bad for a good? Wast thou not vowed and consecrated to God in thy baptism? Are his vows still upon thee? Hast thou "renounced the devil and all his works, the pomps and vanities of this wicked world, and all the sinful lusts of the flesh?" Dost thou feel thyself bound "to keep God's holy will and commandments, and walk in the same all the days of thy life?" Was not this thy baptismal covenant? And hast thou renounced It? Take heed! God is not mocked: that which thou sowest, thou shalt also reap. If thou rob God of thy heart, he will deprive thee of his heaven.
entries.2cb101f66bb65f0ccad90d7f3a432c10f091b015: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen5084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5085" type="x-p"/> Any unclean beast - See on <reference osisRef="Lev.27.2">Lev 27:2</reference> (note).
entries.8b0c0a6a302c1433d66bcda3b649c7b19ed7e8bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen5085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5086" type="x-p"/> Shall add a fifth part - This was probably intended to prevent rash vows and covetous redemptions. The priest alone was to value the thing; and to whatever his valuation was, a fifth part must be added by him who wished to redeem the consecrated thing. Thus, if the priest valued it at forty shekels, if the former owner redeemed it he was obliged to give forty-eight.
entries.24f1a1b1dc5c9079b8908cc7755d8a127b31276e: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen5086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5087" type="x-p"/> Shall sanctify his house - The yearly rent of which, when thus consecrated, went towards the repairs of the tabernacle, which was the house of the Lord.
entries.c3d3c54bddc9b70db8e6603d530fc2ee4c2de0f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen5087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5088" type="x-p"/> Some part of a field - Though the preceding words are not in the text, yet it is generally allowed they should be supplied here, as it was not lawful for a man to vow his whole estate, and thus make his family beggars, in order to enrich the Lord's sanctuary: this God would not permit. The rabbins teach that the land or field, whether good or bad, was valued at forty-eight shekels, for all the years of the jubilee, provided the field was large enough to sow a homer of barley. The חמר chomer was different from the עמר omer: the latter held about three quarts, the former, seventy-five gallons three pints; See the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.16.16">Exo 16:16</reference>. Some suppose that the land was rated, not at fifty shekels for the whole of the years of the jubilee, for this would be but about 3s. per annum; but that it was rated according to its produce, fifty shekels for every homer of barley it produced.
entries.b0f032887dace2e8c66b776fd7cfca64b7933d50: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen5088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5089" type="x-p"/> As a field devoted - It is חרם cherem, a thing so devoted to God as never more to be capable of being redeemed. See on <reference osisRef="Lev.27.29">Lev 27:29</reference> (note).
entries.c696132efc1cf89f7e37a3c59f36a0576a38d5e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen5089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5090" type="x-p"/> Shekel of the sanctuary - A standard shekel; the standard being kept in the sanctuary to try and regulate all the weights in the land by. See <reference osisRef="Gen.20.16">Gen 20:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.23.15">Gen 23:15</reference>.
entries.672bcb541c11403510c6fbf563f4e5429be222b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen5090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5091" type="x-p"/> No devoted thing - shall be sold or redeemed - This is the חרם cherem, which always meant an absolute unredeemable grant to God.
entries.d9f5f2ec933770b819a5cc39ae19178c71a609d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen5091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5092" type="x-p"/> Which shall be devoted of men - Every man who is devoted shall surely be put to death; or, as some understand it, be the Lord's property, or be employed in his service, till death. The law mentioned in these two verses has been appealed to by the enemies of Divine revelation as a proof, that under the Mosaic dispensation human sacrifices were offered to God; but this can never be conceded. Had there been such a law, it certainly would have been more explicitly revealed, and not left in the compass of a few words only, where the meaning is very difficult to be ascertained; and the words themselves differently translated by most interpreters. That there were persons, devoted to destruction under the Mosaic dispensation, is sufficiently evident, for the whole Canaanitish nations were thus devoted by the Supreme Being himself, because the cup of their iniquity was full; but that they were not sacrificed to God, the whole history sufficiently declares. Houbigant understands the passage as speaking of these alone; and says, Non alios licebat anathemate voveri, quam Chananaeos, quos jusserat Deus ad internecionem deleri. "It was not lawful to devote any persons to death but the Canaanites, whom God had commanded to be entirely extirpated." This is perfectly correct; but he might have added that it was because they were the most impure idolaters, and because the cup of their iniquity was full. These God commanded to be put to death; and who can doubt his right to do so, who is the Maker of man, and the Fountain of justice? But what has this to do with human sacrifices? Just nothing. No more than the execution of an ordinary criminal, or a traitor, in the common course of justice, has to do with a sacrifice to God. In the destruction of such idolaters, no religious formality whatever was observed; nor any thing that could give the transaction even the most distant semblance of a sacrifice. In this way Jericho was commanded to be destroyed, <reference osisRef="Jos.6.17">Jos 6:17</reference>, and the Amalekites, <reference osisRef="Deu.25.19">Deu 25:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.3">1Sam 15:3</reference> : but in all these cases the people commanded to be destroyed were such sinners as God's justice did not think proper to spare longer. And has not every system of law the same power? And do we not concede such power to the civil magistrate, for the welfare of the state? God, who is the sovereign arbiter of life and death, acts here in his juridical and legislative capacity; but these are victims to justice, not religious sacrifices. It may be necessary just farther to note that two kinds of vows are mentioned in this chapter: - <div eID="gen5092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5093" type="x-p"/> 1. The נדר neder, (see on Leviticus 7 (note))., which comprehends all those things which, when once devoted, might be redeemed at a certain price, according to the valuation of the priest. <div eID="gen5093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5094" type="x-p"/> 2. The חרם cherem, those things vowed to God of which there remained no power of redemption; they were most holy, i. e., so absolutely devoted to God that they could neither be changed, alienated, nor redeemed: probably because no mental reservation had been made, as in the above case may be supposed. On this ground the word was afterward applied to the most solemn and awful kind of excommunication, meaning a person so entirely devoted to the stroke of vindictive justice, as never to be capable of receiving pardon; and hence the word may be well applied in this sense to the Canaanites, the cup of whose iniquity was full, and who were consigned, without reprieve, to final extermination.
entries.b61fd255908a273533803b57574f58034138f6fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen5094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5095" type="x-p"/> All the tithe of the land - This God claims as his own; and it is spoken of here as being a point perfectly settled, and concerning which there was neither doubt nor difficulty. See my view of this subject <reference osisRef="Gen.28.22">Gen 28:22</reference> (note), to which I do not see the necessity of adding any thing.
entries.e7a90afd44875ef1b87900206e47ab7f17047a06: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen5095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5096" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever passeth under the rod - The signification of this verse is well given by the rabbins: "When a man was to give the tithe of his sheep or calves to God, he was to shut up the whole flock in one fold, in which there was one narrow door capable of letting out one at a time. The owner, about to give the tenth to the Lord, stood by the door with a rod in his hand, the end of which was dipped in vermilion or red ochre. The mothers of those lambs or calves stood without: the door being opened, the young ones ran out to join themselves to their dams; and as they passed out the owner stood with his rod over them, and counted one, two, three, four, five, etc., and when the tenth came, he touched it with the coloured rod, by which it was distinguished to be the tithe calf, sheep, etc., and whether poor or lean, perfect or blemished, that was received as the legitimate tithe." It seems to be in reference to this custom that the Prophet Ezekiel, speaking to Israel, says: I will cause you to pass under the rod, and will bring you into the bond of the covenant - you shall be once more claimed as the Lord's property, and be in all things devoted to his service, being marked or ascertained, by especial providences and manifestations of his kindness, to be his peculiar people.
entries.51f754d61e55cc80def66244cfad593717cbf453: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen5096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5097" type="x-p"/> These are the commandments - This conclusion is very similar to that at the end of the preceding chapter. I have already supposed that this chapter should have followed the 25th, and that the 26th originally terminated the book. Mr. Ainsworth, the whole of whose writings are animated with the spirit of piety, concludes this book with the following excellent remarks: - "The tithes in Israel being thus sanctified by the commandment of God to his honor, the maintenance of his ministers, and the relief of the poor, it taught them and teaches us to honor the Lord with our substance, (<reference osisRef="Pro.3.9">Pro 3:9</reference>), acknowledging him to be the author of all our increase and store; (<reference osisRef="Deu.8.13-Deu.8.18">Deu 8:13-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.8">Hos 2:8</reference>); to honor his Ministers, and to communicate unto them in all good things, (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17">1Tim 5:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.18">1Tim 5:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.6">Gal 6:6</reference>), that they who sow unto us spiritual things should reap our carnal things, (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.11">1Cor 9:11</reference>), and to give Alms of such things as we have, that all things may be clear unto us, (<reference osisRef="Luk.11.41">Luk 11:41</reference>), yea, even to sell that we have, and give alms; to provide ourselves bags that wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not. <reference osisRef="Luk.12.33">Luk 12:33</reference>." They who forget their Maker, his ministers, and the poor, are never likely to hear that blessed word in the great day: "Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you; for I was hungry, and ye gave me meat; thirsty, and ye gave me drink; naked, and ye clothed me; sick and in prison, and ye came unto me." <div eID="gen5097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5098" type="x-p"/> Reader, thou hast now gone through the whole of this most interesting book; a book whose subject is too little regarded by Christians in general. Here thou mayest discover the rigid requisitions of Divine justice, the sinfulness of sin, the exceeding breadth of the commandment, and the end of all human perfection. And now what thinkest thou of that word, "Whatsoever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law?" <reference osisRef="Rom.3.19">Rom 3:19</reference>. But who are under the law - the condemning power of the pure, rigid, moral law of God? Not the Jews only, but every soul of man: all to whom it is sent, and who acknowledge it as a Divine revelation, and have not been redeemed from the guilt of sin by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ; for "cursed is every one that continueth not in all things that are written in the book of the law to do them." By this law then is the knowledge, but not the cure, of sin. Here then what God saith unto thee: "If therefore perfection were by the Levitical priesthood, (for under it the people received the law), what farther need was there that another priest should rise after the order of Melchisedec, and not be called after the order of Aaron? For the priesthood being changed, there is made of necessity a change also of the law; <reference osisRef="Heb.7.11">Heb 7:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.12">Heb 7:12</reference>. Now of the things which we have spoken, this is the sum: We have such a high priest, who is set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens; a minister of the sanctuary, and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man; <reference osisRef="Heb.8.1">Heb 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.2">Heb 8:2</reference>. For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.4">Heb 10:4</reference>. But Christ being come a high priest of good things to come, - neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood, he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us. And for this cause he is the Mediator of the New Testament, that, by means of death, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance. And without shedding of blood is no remission. So Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many, and unto them that look for him shall he appear the second time, without sin, unto salvation;" <reference osisRef="Heb.9.11">Heb 9:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">Heb 9:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.15">Heb 9:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.22">Heb 9:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">Heb 9:28</reference>. We see then that Christ was the End of the law for righteousness (for justification) to every one that believeth. "Unto him, therefore, who hath loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood, and hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father; to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen." <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Rev 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Rev 1:6</reference>. <div eID="gen5098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5099" type="x-p"/> Sections in the Book of
